title: Industrializing reactive capture of CO2 - Nature Energy
gist: A Nature Energy Perspective from University of Toronto and Shell Global Solutions argues that reactive capture of CO2 (RCC) — feeding CO2-rich capture liquids straight into an electrolyser instead of thermally regenerating the solvent — could be the first electrified CO2-conversion route to reach industrial adoption, even at today's selectivity and voltage, provided stability and scale barriers are solved. The named bottlenecks are solvent-tolerant cathodes, electrolysis-compatible capture fluids, and bipolar membrane efficiency, scalability and durability.

insights.claim: Reactive capture of CO2 (RCC) feeds CO2-rich capture liquids directly into an electrolyser, eliminating the thermal regeneration step that conventional amine capture requires before the CO2 can be used.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Removing the thermal stripper removes a major heat load and a large capex block from capture-to-fuels projects — watch whether capture-solvent vendors and electrolyser developers start pitching integrated units rather than bolt-on conversion.
insights.quote: Reactive capture of CO2 (RCC) feeds CO2-rich liquids directly into an electrolyser, bypassing thermal regeneration and simplifying process integration.

insights.claim: RCC electrolysers tolerate industrial impurities better than gas-fed CO2 electrolysers and can still produce high-purity gaseous outputs, making them suited to real industrial CO2 feedstocks rather than purified CO2.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Impurity tolerance is the practical gate on deploying CO2 conversion at cement, steel and refinery sites; a route that skips upstream gas polishing shortens the path from pilot to plant.
insights.quote: RCC has a greater tolerance to industrial impurities and can generate high-purity gaseous outputs, enabling a fully electrified chemical synthesis process that is suited to industrial CO2 feedstocks

insights.claim: The commercial pitch for reactive capture is a fully electrified chemical synthesis process — capture and conversion driven by electricity alone — rather than an electrochemical step bolted onto a heat-driven capture plant.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Full electrification shifts the cost driver from steam/heat to power price and grid access, changing which sites and geographies are viable and linking project economics to electricity markets.

insights.claim: The argued path to viability is that RCC can win early industrial adoption ahead of other electrified CO2-conversion routes at present levels of selectivity and voltage — meaning integration advantages, not catalyst breakthroughs, are the decisive variable.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Contrarian to the usual 'wait for better catalysts' framing: it implies capital should follow stack engineering, membranes and solvent chemistry rather than another round of catalyst selectivity gains.
insights.quote: RCC could become viable for early industrial adoption—ahead of other electrified routes and at present levels of selectivity and voltage—if stability and scale barriers are addressed
insights.locator: In this Perspective we argue that RCC

insights.claim: Near-term deployment of electrified CO2 capture and conversion is framed as depending on integration with existing energy infrastructure rather than on greenfield build-out.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Retrofit-compatible technologies get to revenue first; screen CCU startups on whether their unit drops into an existing capture loop or demands a new plant.
insights.quote: near-term deployment depends on integration with current energy infrastructure

insights.claim: RCC electrolysers are explicitly acknowledged as less technologically developed than gas-fed CO2 electrolysers, so the case for RCC rests on system-level advantages rather than device maturity.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A maturity gap means longer time-to-bankability and more technology risk in RCC-based ventures than headline integration benefits suggest — price the TRL gap.
insights.quote: current RCC electrolysers are less developed than their gas-fed counterparts

insights.claim: Progress in reactive capture is pinned to three specific engineering problems: solvent-tolerant cathodes, electrolysis-compatible capture fluids, and bipolar membrane efficiency, scalability and durability.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: This is a ready-made diligence checklist — a company claiming RCC readiness that has not solved all three is not de-risked, and the membrane suppliers sit on a chokepoint.
insights.quote: Progress will depend on engineering solvent-tolerant cathodes, formulating electrolysis-compatible capture fluids and advancing bipolar membrane efficiency, scalability and durability.

insights.claim: Bipolar membranes are treated as the make-or-break component for reactive capture, with a dedicated figure comparing cation-exchange membranes (CEM) against bipolar membranes (BPM) for RCC electrolysers.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Membrane choice is an investable sub-sector: BPM durability and water-dissociation efficiency gate the whole RCC stack, so membrane makers capture value regardless of which electrolyser brand wins.
insights.quote: Fig. 4: Comparison of CEM and BPM for RCC electrolysers.

insights.claim: The stated barriers to RCC viability are stability and scale — not selectivity or energy efficiency — which relocates the risk from lab chemistry to durability testing and cell-area scale-up.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Watch for published multi-thousand-hour stability runs and pilot-scale cell areas as the real milestones; anything short of those is not evidence of industrialization.
insights.locator: In this Perspective we argue that RCC

insights.claim: The Perspective evaluates the performance targets RCC must hit to become cost-competitive with alternative CO2-conversion technologies, and anchors that in a techno-economic synthesis of sustainable syngas pathways.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Syngas is the chosen benchmark product, so RCC economics will be judged against reverse water-gas shift, methane reforming and solid-oxide routes — use those as the comparison set when modelling any RCC play.
insights.quote: Fig. 3: Techno-economic synthesis of sustainable syngas pathways.

insights.claim: The state of the art in reactive capture splits into two competing solvent chemistries — hydroxide-based and amine-based RCC — which are benchmarked separately, implying no consensus yet on which capture fluid wins.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: An unsettled chemistry standard means early equipment bets carry stranding risk; favour developers whose cathode and membrane stack is not locked to one solvent family.
insights.quote: Fig. 2: State-of-the-art hydroxide-based and amine-based RCC reports.

insights.claim: The cited literature holds that electrolyser energy dominates separation costs in state-of-the-art CO2 electrolysers, which is the cost logic behind favouring a route that produces high-purity gaseous outputs directly.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: If energy, not downstream separation, is the dominant cost, cheap firm power and low cell voltage are the levers that decide project returns — model power price sensitivity first.
insights.quote: Electrolyzer energy dominates separation costs in state-of-the-art CO2 electrolyzers: implications for single-pass CO2 utilization.

insights.claim: Shell Global Solutions International B.V. both funded this work and supplied three co-authors based in Amsterdam who provided the industrial insights, signalling that a supermajor is actively evaluating reactive capture rather than only academic groups.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Oil-major co-authorship on a 'path to industrialization' Perspective is an early corporate-interest tell — track Shell's CCU pilot announcements and any electrolyser partnerships as follow-on signal.
insights.quote: K.H., P.-E.J. and P.J.C. are employees of Shell Global Solutions International B.V.

insights.claim: The research base sits in Canada, with the University of Toronto group supported by the Canada Research Chairs Program and NSERC Alliance and Discovery funding alongside industrial partner Hatch.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Geographic concentration of RCC expertise points to where spinouts and licensing deals are most likely to originate.
